x.A: AWS manages the RDS infrastructure layer, operating system, and platform, so this isn't the customer's responsibility.
x.B: Creating the DB instance and configuring its maintenance window are customer choices, so the operations team handles them.
x.C: With ECS on EC2, customers manage the additional software on the hosts, such as monitoring, patch management, log management, and intrusion detection.
x.D: RDS handles patching of the database engine within the managed service, so the team doesn't install patches themselves.
x.E: AWS is responsible for the physical security of its data centers.
x.F: Direct Connect isn't encrypted by default, so the customer must encrypt data in transit, for example with a VPN or MACsec.

x.A: Fargate would be charged for every run, but it adds containerization work and has a minimum billing per task, and Lambda is cheaper for a 10 second job.
x.B: A Lambda function with 1 GB of memory runs only for the 10 seconds the job needs, scheduled hourly by EventBridge. You pay only for those seconds, so it's the lowest cost.
x.C: Running a container in an AMI on the existing instance still keeps the instance running, so you pay for the server all the time.
x.D: Stopping and starting the instance hourly adds startup time and still costs more than Lambda, and it's complex to manage.

x.A: A vault lock in governance mode lets users with sufficient permissions change or remove the lock, so the files could be altered during retention.
x.B: Data Lifecycle Manager creates EBS snapshot policies and doesn't cover S3 buckets or lock the backups.
x.C: S3 File Gateway isn't a backup service for EC2 and S3, and lifecycle management doesn't prevent altering files.
x.D: AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode makes backups immutable for the retention period, so nobody can delete or change them, and AWS Backup covers both EC2 and S3.

x.A: Systems Manager Inventory collects metadata about managed instances and doesn't map relationships across all accounts' workloads.
x.B: Collecting workload details with Step Functions and drawing diagrams by hand is a lot of manual effort.
x.C: Workload Discovery on AWS automatically builds architecture diagrams that show how resources relate across accounts and Regions, with no manual work.
x.D: X-Ray traces requests in applications and doesn't build a resource inventory map across accounts.

x.A: The budget amount is set when creating the budget in AWS Budgets, not in the Cost and Usage Reports section.
x.B: A budget is created in AWS Budgets, with the amount set in the budget. Setting it for the required accounts through the billing dashboards fits the requirement.
x.C: Budget actions need a role that AWS Budgets can assume, not an IAM user.
x.D: An IAM role for AWS Budgets with the required permissions lets Budgets run the budget actions on your behalf.
x.E: An AWS Config rule isn't what a budget action applies. Config rules only evaluate compliance and don't stop provisioning.
x.F: The alert plus a budget action that applies an SCP prevents provisioning of additional resources when the threshold is met.

x.A: Running a similar set of EC2 instances in the second Region costs a lot, since they run all the time.
x.B: EBS snapshots copied manually or by script can work, but that needs ongoing management and doesn't give central control of backups for EC2 instances.
x.C: AWS Backup centrally manages backup plans and can copy EC2 backups to another Region, so you only pay for backup storage. It's the most cost-effective.
x.D: Running duplicate instances in the second Region costs more, and DataSync isn't a backup tool for EC2 instances.

x.A: DataSync doesn't support the AS2 protocol.
x.B: AppFlow transfers data between SaaS applications and AWS services and doesn't support AS2.
x.C: Transfer Family supports the AS2 protocol and can use a Lambda function as a custom identity provider to authenticate users against the company's IdP.
x.D: Storage Gateway doesn't support AS2, and a Cognito identity pool isn't used to authenticate to an external IdP for transfers.

x.A: EC2 means managing servers, which is more administrative effort.
x.B: Lambda runs the computation without servers, and it can be configured with 1 GB of memory and enough ephemeral storage, so it needs very little administration.
x.C: RDS provides the relational database as a managed service, so it needs little administration.
x.D: DynamoDB is NoSQL, not a relational format.
x.E: EKS involves managing Kubernetes, which is more effort.

x.A: Activating a user-defined cost allocation tag named department in the management account applies it to all member accounts. Cost Explorer can then group by the tag and filter by EC2 to show spending by department across accounts.
x.B: The department tag is user-defined, because the company's tagging policy created it. AWS-defined tags are things like aws:createdBy.
x.C: Member accounts can't activate cost allocation tags for the whole organization. This must be done in the management account.
x.D: The tag isn't AWS-defined, and member accounts can't activate it for the organization.

x.A: Lambda functions need custom code for the Salesforce API, plus error handling, so it's more effort.
x.B: Step Functions orchestrate steps but would still need tasks that call Salesforce, which means building them.
x.C: AppFlow is a managed integration service with a Salesforce connector. It transfers data to S3 with encryption in transit, and it can use a KMS customer managed key for encryption at rest.
x.D: A custom connector means building and maintaining the connector, which is more effort when a built-in connector exists.

x.A: An ALB supports HTTP and HTTPS only and can't handle UDP or generic TCP, so it can't be used for the game traffic.
x.B: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes users over the AWS network to the nearest endpoint. It supports TCP and UDP, and an NLB handles both protocols for the EC2 instances.
x.C: CloudFront doesn't support UDP traffic.
x.D: CloudFront and ALB don't support UDP, so this doesn't work.

x.A: SNS can't deliver to a database endpoint, and a bigger instance doesn't fix reliability.
x.B: An SQS queue stores orders durably, so none are lost during surges. Auto Scaling workers behind the queue process them into Aurora as fast as needed.
x.C: SNS can't be read from by instances, and you can't subscribe a database endpoint to a topic.
x.D: Writing to the queue only when CPU is high is inconsistent, and scheduled scaling doesn't react to actual traffic.

x.A: A Glue Scala job has a startup time and minimum charges that make it costly for a 30 second job on 2 MB of data.
x.B: EMR with Spark needs a cluster, which is costly and slow to start for tiny jobs.
x.C: Lambda with Python can run with 1 GB of memory and finishes in 30 seconds, triggered by the S3 upload. You pay only for the run time, so it's the cheapest and fastest.
x.D: Glue PySpark has the same startup and minimum billing costs, so it's expensive for small files.

x.A: Modifying the instance to Multi-AZ creates a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover, and the endpoint stays the same, so no application code changes are required.
x.B: Creating a new deployment and restoring a snapshot changes the endpoint and causes downtime and data loss, so it isn't minimal downtime.
x.C: A read replica is read-only and doesn't fail over automatically, and Route 53 weighted records would send writes to a read-only replica.
x.D: RDS can't be placed in an Auto Scaling group.

x.A: gp3 volumes don't support EBS Multi-Attach.
x.B: st1 volumes don't support Multi-Attach.
x.C: Multi-Attach is supported on io1 and io2 Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes on Nitro instances in the same AZ, so multiple instances can write to the volume at once.
x.D: gp2 volumes don't support Multi-Attach.

x.A: Multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling with an ALB spreads the stateless application tier across AZs and routes traffic only to healthy instances. Together with the Multi-AZ database, the whole application is highly available.
x.B: Snapshots sent to another Region help with backups, but they don't make the application highly available.
x.C: Latency-based routing doesn't add redundancy for the EC2 tier if all instances are in a single AZ.
x.D: A Multi-AZ ALB doesn't help if the EC2 instances are still in a single AZ.

x.A: Discount sharing is controlled from the management account, not from a member account.
x.B: Turning on discount sharing in the management account lets other accounts in the organization use unused Savings Plan commitments, so the full benefit is used.
x.C: Moving workloads between accounts is manual work that discount sharing avoids.
x.D: Savings Plans can't be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

x.A: A WebSocket API is for two-way real-time communication, not for REST APIs.
x.B: A REST API in API Gateway with a private VPC link to the ECS services lets the frontend reach the containers in private subnets without exposing them.
x.C: A WebSocket API doesn't match the REST requirement, and API Gateway can't be given access with a security group.
x.D: API Gateway isn't placed in a VPC, so a security group can't give it access to private ECS services. A VPC link is needed.

x.A: Replication copies objects to another bucket and doesn't transition storage classes.
x.B: Moving to Standard-IA would add retrieval fees if the objects are accessed unpredictably.
x.C: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on use, with no retrieval fees, so it suits unpredictable access patterns.
x.D: S3 Inventory is unneeded, and there's no direct way to transition objects with it. A lifecycle rule does the transition.

x.A: A NAT gateway is for IPv4 traffic, and these instances use IPv6 addresses.
x.B: An internet gateway allows both outbound and inbound connections, so external services could initiate connections.
x.C: A virtual private gateway is for VPN or Direct Connect to on-premises, not for internet access.
x.D: An egress-only internet gateway allows outbound IPv6 traffic from instances and blocks connections initiated from the internet.

x.A: Intelligent-Tiering reduces storage costs for varying access but doesn't affect network paths or data transfer.
x.B: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers and adds a fee, and traffic still goes over the internet.
x.C: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 is free and keeps traffic between the VPC and S3 on the AWS network, so it minimizes cost and avoids the internet. Associating it with the route tables makes the containers use it.
x.D: Interface endpoints for S3 have hourly and per-GB charges, so with 1 TB a day they cost more than the free gateway endpoint.

x.A: DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond reads and API compatibility. Only the endpoint in the code needs to change.
x.B: DynamoDB doesn't have read replicas that you point an application at.
x.C: More RCUs adds throughput but doesn't lower read latency to microseconds.
x.D: ElastiCache would require application changes to implement the caching logic, which is more work than DAX.

x.A: CloudFront caches static files at edge locations, so fewer requests reach the ALB and EC2 instances, which lowers cost and improves latency.
x.B: ElastiCache can't be connected to an ALB to serve cached files.
x.C: WAF filters requests and doesn't cache static files.
x.D: A second ALB in another Region adds cost and doesn't cache content.

x.A: A full mesh of VPC peering connections across Regions grows quickly and needs a lot of administration.
x.B: Direct Connect gateways connect on-premises networks to VPCs, not VPCs to one another in this way.
x.C: A transit gateway in each Region connects the VPCs in that Region, and transit gateway peering connects the Regions. It's a hub-and-spoke design with the least administration.
x.D: PrivateLink exposes specific services privately, and it doesn't provide full connectivity among all VPCs.

x.A: FSx for Windows File Server is for Windows SMB workloads and doesn't suit ECS Linux containers in the same way, and it doesn't offer a mount target in every AZ as EFS does.
x.B: FSx for NetApp ONTAP isn't the AWS Backup cross-Region choice for this scenario, and it's more costly.
x.C: EFS Standard stores data across multiple AZs, provides a mount target in each AZ, and AWS Backup can replicate it to another Region on a schedule that meets an 8 hour RPO.
x.D: FSx for OpenZFS isn't a Multi-AZ file system with a mount target in each AZ in the same way.
